answer:
**Verdict:** Don't drop out because you have an idea. Stay in school and build it on the side. Drop out only if the side project takes off by itself, meaning real users want it and it's eating your life. At that point Paul Graham thinks running with it is reasonable.

**Based on:** he said it, to Stanford students in 2014, and repeated the core of it in an August 2026 essay. Applying "takes off" to your case is inferred from what he said (confidence: medium).

**Why he'd say it**
- **You can't do both.** "you can't start up a startup as a student, because if you start a startup you're not a student anymore." ([Before the Startup, 2014 @ 18:22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1102s)). In 2026 he still says: "Running a startup is incompatible with being a full time student." ([How Universities Should Prepare Founders](https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html))
- **At 20 it's too early.** "Do not start a startup in college." He adds: "20 is not the optimal time to do it." (@ [18:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1136s))
- **Waiting costs you nothing.** "You're not sacrificing anything if you forego starting a startup at 20, cuz you'll be more likely to succeed if you wait." (@ 21:12) He thinks your early twenties are for chasing projects "on a whim that seem like they have no payoff", and that success would take that freedom away. His example is Zuckerberg: "Facebook is running him as much as he is running Facebook." (@ 19:32, 20:40)
- **The exception is the important part.** If a side project takes off: "Then you face the choice of either running with it or not, and maybe it's reasonable to run with it." (@ [21:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1272s)) He gives the sign to watch for: "You will know that it's becoming a real startup when it takes over an alarming percentage of your life" (@ [43:15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=2595s)).
- **In 2026 he leans more toward the exception.** He points out that Microsoft and Meta "both got started during reading period at Harvard". He wants universities to give students free time for side projects, since many of them "would be incipient startups." When one takes off, he puts it bluntly: "Are the students just supposed to abandon them? Because it's either that or drop out." So his answer has moved from "wait" toward "build on the side and see if it takes off". It hasn't moved to "drop out for an idea".

**How this applies to you**
1. He separates an *idea* from a *side project that's taking off*. You have an idea, so you're in the first group.
2. He doesn't trust ideas you set out to think up. He says they tend to be "not only bad, but bad and plausible sounding" (@ [24:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1474s)). Building it is how you find out which kind yours is.
3. The first thing he asks founders is their growth rate. So the test for dropping out isn't how good the idea feels. It's whether users keep showing up and growth keeps coming without you pushing.

**What he's done:** He co-founded YC, which started as a summer program so students could try a startup without leaving school. Sam Altman was a Stanford sophomore in the first batch, in 2005.

**What would change his answer:** Real growth with users who want the product, so that school is now what's getting in the way. If that happens, he'd say running with it is reasonable, and in 2026 he treats dropping out as the natural result.

**Caveat:** The vault flags that his advice to students comes from YC's founder, who has a stake in the YC model. His 2026 essay was written to universities, not students, so it never says outright "you should drop out".

**Verdict:** Keep building on what you have until you have growth to show, then raise from strength. Don't raise now on a pitch. Revenue isn't the real bar, though. Growth is, and if you need some money to reach your next milestone, raise just enough to get there.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: high). His rules on this are explicit and repeated across sources from 2014 to 2026. He never answered "raise vs. bootstrap" as a binary.

**How we get there**
1. **Traction is what convinces investors, not pitching.** "the best way to convince investors, is to start a startup that's actually doing well, meaning ... growing fast, and then simply tell investors so." ([Before the Startup, 2014 @ 9:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=591s)) And: "Someone who knows zero about fund raising but has made something users really love will have an easier time raising money." (@ [13:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=797s))
2. **Spend what you have to reach a milestone, then raise.** In September 2026 he said: "I think you can still start a startup on not much money." "So you just do what you can on the money you got. As long as you can get to some kind of milestone, then you can convince investors to give you more." ([PG on Startups, Ambition, and Great Founders @ 11:37–12:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=697s))
3. **Fundraising is secondary.** "Fundraising is merely a necessary evil. The people you need to impress are users, not investors, and the way you impress them is with prototypes, not words." ([How Universities Should Prepare Founders, 2026](https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html))

Put together: raising now, with nothing growing, means pitching on words, which is the weakest position you can raise from. Building first is his default.

**Why "until I have revenue" is slightly the wrong bar**
- The first question he asks founders is their growth rate, not revenue ([[thinking/pg]]). Revenue growing week over week is ideal evidence. Users growing fast with a plan to charge also counts.
- He's not against bootstrapping as such, but he's a venture person. He'd want you to raise once growth makes it easy, not hold out for profitability on principle.
- Selling at a loss to fake traction doesn't count: "If your product is a $10 bill that you sell for $5, your growth rate isn't telling you anything useful." ([[product/pricing/charging-from-the-start]])
- A small check just to buy time is fine in his world. Livingston describes YC's original deal as money "just so a Founder can sort of quit their job pay the rent and test out if their idea even works before they then go on to raise Venture Capital Money" ([How YC Was Created @ 2:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY&t=170s)).

**What others at YC have done:** Seibel spent about eight months failing to raise for Justin.tv. With two months of runway left, the team switched to making it profitable, and he says they got more done in those two months than in all the months of pitching ([How Founders Win at Fundraising @ 6:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=404s)).

**What would change his answer:**
- **You can't reach a convincing milestone without capital.** Hardware, rockets and expensive compute are examples. Then raise now, but only enough for the next stage ("even a rocket startup you can start on not much money because what you do is you adjust for how much money you've got").
- **You're already a recognised expert in your field.** He notes such founders come with "automatic cred" and can raise on very little.
- **You already have fast growth.** Then you're in the "simply tell investors so" position: raise now.

**Not in the vault:** his essays *Ramen Profitable* (2009) and *Default Alive or Default Dead* (2015) are the closest he comes to this exact question. Both point the same way: get to where you can survive on revenue, because then you raise with leverage rather than out of need. The vault hasn't ingested them, so treat this as my recollection, not a cited quote.

**Caveats:** PG co-founded YC and is an investor, so he leans toward "raise eventually, for growth." And the vault records him saying "if you raise money, don't think the next time you raise money it's gonna be so easy" (2014). That's another reason not to raise before you have something real.

**Verdict:** Go to San Francisco, at least for a while. PG says this is "the same now as it always is", and he'd tell a Berlin founder exactly what he told a Stockholm audience in April 2026: go, and come back later if you want to. He thinks the best way to do that is through YC.

**Based on:** said it. He gave this talk to European founders in a European city, so the only difference for you is the city's name.

**Why he'd say it**
- **It's a flat yes.** "Should I go there? And the answer is the same now as it always is. Yes, you should. You can go there for a bit and then come back, but you should at least go." ([[yt-QHJkUw31YX8]] @ 0:36, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=36s)
- **Every field has one center.** Paris was the center for painting, Göttingen for math, Hollywood for movies. Being ambitious works the same way "when you're moving across a dotted line on a map" (@ 1:09).
- **Peers.** "The people are better, and there's also a lot more of them." (@ 1:09) Chance meetings with people doing the same work count for more than planned ones: "if you're working on something ambitious, there's nothing in the world that's better than serendipitous meetings with people who are working on the same stuff." (@ 3:20)
- **Investors.** "Investors outside Silicon Valley implicitly assume that any local startup is second rate. It's not a uniquely Swedish problem. It's the same everywhere." Going to the Valley flips this, so your standing goes up back home too (@ 6:39, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=399s). He also says Valley investors decide much faster, because competition means good deals don't wait.
- **What it does to you.** "When you're a big fish in a small pond, you don't even know how big a fish you are." (@ 8:52) Seeing successful founders up close turns a goal that seemed impossible into "just a hard one" (@ 10:34).
- **Culture.** "In Silicon Valley, people help you for no reason." (@ 12:15)
- **Staying vs. going home.** "startups that go back home after YC are only about half as likely to become unicorns." (@ 18:57, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1137s) He discounts this himself because of selection bias: the founders who stay also tend to be the more confident and determined ones.

**If you care about Berlin:** his advice for building up a home ecosystem is still to go and come back. Returning founders bring better companies, Valley money and Valley culture (@ 16:10–16:42). He also says the title of "Silicon Valley of Europe" is "still up for grabs". All a city needs is "a place founders want to live and a critical mass of them" (@ 20:04–21:09).

**What he's done:** YC used to fly its Boston-batch startups to the Valley for a second demo day because Boston investors wouldn't fund them. That trip is where Dropbox met Sequoia (@ 7:43).

**What would change his answer:** He never says you have to stay forever. The one counterweight he gives is personal: "Money isn't everything. Once you have kids, you'll find you care more about them than your company." (@ 19:30) Family is the only reason he gives for going home; he gives none for never going at all.

**Caveats:**
- He's the founder of YC, so he's recommending the place where YC operates, and he admits he's "talking my own book" when he suggests doing YC.
- The unicorn statistic is YC's internal data as he reports it. He shows no numbers or method.
- Sam Altman (July 2026) agrees that moving to SF is still probably good advice, but says he has "less of an intuition for it now" ([[yt-ZIaOBAjvc38]], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38).
- Nothing in the vault mentions Berlin by name.

**Verdict:** Paul Graham would tell you to keep going on the goal and pivot the means, which means your co-founder may be right. Being "persistent" counts only if you're committed to the users and problem you chose. If what you want to keep is the current product or approach, he'd call that obstinacy, not persistence.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). The vault has nothing from PG on two co-founders disagreeing about a pivot. His 2024 essay on persistence and obstinacy settles the question, though, and his other writing supports it.

**How we get there**
1. **His nearest case:** in "The Right Kind of Stubborn" ([paulgraham.com/persistence.html](https://paulgraham.com/persistence.html)) he separates the two: "The persistent are attached to the goal. The obstinate are attached to their ideas about how to reach it." He sees them as different kinds of behaviour, not the same behaviour judged by how things turned out.
2. **The rule behind it:** "You'll give way on any point low down in the decision tree, if its expected value drops sufficiently, but energy and resilience keep pushing you toward whatever you chose higher up." He also says "persistence often requires that one change one's mind."
3. **Applied to you:** so "pivot or persist?" is the wrong split. The real question is what the pivot changes.
   - If it keeps the same users and problem and changes the solution, it's a move low in the decision tree. PG would make it if the evidence says the current approach isn't working.
   - If it drops your users and problem for something your co-founder just finds more appealing, that's a change at the top of the tree. There he says "It's ok to be irrational near the top of the decision tree," so sticking with a problem you love is legitimate.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Watch how you react to criticism.** His test for obstinacy is how someone responds when you point out a problem. The Collisons "not only listen, but listen with an almost predatory intensity," and most successful people "are never more engaged than when you disagree with them." Your co-founder pushing for a pivot is exactly that situation. If you're tuning them out, that's the warning sign.
- **Look at the numbers before deciding.** "I always begin by asking founders their growth rate. It shows whether they've built the right thing." ([paulgraham.com/earn.html](https://paulgraham.com/earn.html)) If you're growing well, the pivot needs a strong case. If you're flat, your attachment needs one.
- **Ask whether the pivot is a "tail that could wag the dog."** If your co-founder wants to move toward something users already use or ask for, PG takes that seriously. PayPal was built as a demo for security software until eBay sellers started using it, and "after a couple months the founders acknowledged that this was the business they were now in" ([paulgraham.com/powerful.html](https://paulgraham.com/powerful.html)). A pivot pulled by users is very different from one pushed by boredom.
- **He backs founders, not ideas:** "startups' ideas are very mutable" ([YC interview @ 20:27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=1227s)). He doesn't think the original idea deserves your loyalty.
- **A YC partner on the same point (Michael Seibel, not PG):** "hold the problem you're solving tightly, hold the customer tightly, hold the solution you're building loosely." ([How to Plan an MVP @ 3:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=199s))

**What would change his answer:** if the current approach is still working (decent growth, users pulling you forward), or if the pivot gives up the problem you both chose rather than a failed solution, his rule says persist. The inference could break because his essay is about one person's stubbornness, not two co-founders disagreeing. He never said whose judgement should win between partners.

On the co-founder relationship itself, the vault has only Dalton Caldwell and Michael Seibel ([YC video, 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U)), not PG. They trace most co-founder fights to a lack of mutual respect for the other person's judgement. That's a reason to treat this as a question you settle together with evidence, not as a contest of wills.

**Verdict:** Paul Graham would tell you to launch the tiny version this week. You only learn whether you've made something people want once real users have it, and a full-featured product you haven't launched only delays that test.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: high). None of the PG sources in the vault say "launch fast" in those words. But several of his rules lead straight to it, and the other YC partners in the vault do say it outright.

**How we get there**
1. He thinks the only real test is users, and that you win them with working products, not plans: "The people you need to impress are users, not investors, and the way you impress them is with prototypes, not words." ([How Universities Should Prepare Founders](https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html))
2. In September 2026 he said shipping too slowly is still the common failure, even with AI tools: "we have all these powerful AI tools and there's still a lot of startups in this batch that are not shipping fast enough." ([YC interview @ 16:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=964s)) He agreed with the host that shipping pace is the best predictor of success. That wording is the host's, though, and PG just said "Yeah."
3. He steers a company by its growth rate: "I always begin by asking founders their growth rate. It shows whether they've built the right thing." You have no growth rate until you've launched, so building the full product first means flying without that compass.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Startups are counterintuitive.** "startups are so weird that if you follow your instincts they will lead you astray." ([Before the Startup @ 2:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=137s)) Wanting to polish before launching is exactly the kind of instinct he means.
- **You learn by doing.** "you'll learn faster if you just do it." ([Before the Startup @ 33:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=2016s))
- **Start human, then work toward perfect.** He said this about how AI developed, not about launching. It's an analogy, not his advice on this question: "instead of starting with perfect and then working your way up to human, you start with human and then work your way towards perfect." ([YC interview @ 13:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=829s))
- **Hold the goal fixed and the means loose.** The full feature list is a means. Users will show you which parts of it matter.

**The rest of YC says it directly**
- Michael Seibel: "if you can walk away from one thing from this presentation, it's launch something bad quickly." He also defines launching as "when you get any customers," not a press event. ([How to Plan an MVP @ 1:41](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=101s))
- Dalton Caldwell (2026) argues that AI makes this matter more, not less. He built a "crazy huge thing" in two weeks, then "had to delete 80% of the features" before people understood it and signed up. His advice is to add features only when "users are pulling you towards building more stuff." ([How to Build an MVP in the AI Coding Era @ 1:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rQtrzBcf_Us&t=66s))

**Not in the vault:** PG has written "release early" advice directly in older essays, such as "The Hardest Lessons for Startups to Learn." The vault doesn't include those essays yet, so I haven't quoted them. Adding them would turn this from an inference into a direct quote.

**What would change his answer:** a product where a weak first version is useless or dangerous. Seibel names regulated fields like banking and insurance, and hard tech, as cases where you can't launch this fast. PG also says a product half as good as a competitor's gets "no customers," which matters if users already have a good alternative. Even then, the YC answer is to make the first version narrower, not to wait longer.

**Verdict:** Start the startup now. Paul Graham used to give the "work somewhere for a few years first" advice. By 2014 he said publicly that it was a mistake, and he still holds that view in 2026: the way to learn how to start a startup is to start one.

**Based on:** he said it (confidence: high). He addressed this exact choice and has repeated the reasoning in several sources since.

**Why he'd say it**
- He retracted the "job first" advice himself: "One of the things I got wrong early on, is that I advised people who were interested in starting a startup to go work for some other company for a few years before starting their own." ([Before the Startup, Stanford 2014 @ 33:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=2016s))
- The reason, in the same passage: "the best way to learn how to start a startup is to try and start it. You may not be successful, but you'll learn faster if you just do it." (@ 33:36)
- He repeated it in 2026: "The only way to learn how to start a startup is to do it." ([How Universities Should Prepare Founders](https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html))
- What a big company teaches is the wrong thing. He dismisses business school because it teaches management, "a problem that you only have in a startup if you're sufficiently successful" (2014 @ [33:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1985s)). The hard part is product: "knowing what to build, and being able to build it" (2026). A few years at Google mostly teaches how a large company works, which by the same logic is the wrong lesson. That last step is my application of his reasoning, not something he said about Google.
- Take risks while you're young. "The solution is to take multiple shots. Which is another reason to start taking risks early." He adds that work needing a huge amount of time and energy is best done "when you're young and don't yet have children." ([Superlinear Returns, 2023](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html))
- You don't need a job to learn something: "You don't necessarily need a job doing x in order to work on x; often you can just start doing it in some form yourself." He also warns: "You'll become like whoever you work with." ([When To Do What You Love, 2024](https://paulgraham.com/when.html))

**What would change his answer**
- **You're still a full-time student.** He would tell you to finish first, or to work on side projects. In 2014 he said "Do not start a startup in college" ([@ 18:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1136s)), and in 2026 he still says a startup and full-time study don't mix.
- **You can't afford the risk, or you don't really want the high-variance life.** "Exposing oneself to superlinear returns is not for everyone. Most people will be better off as part of the pool." He says it suits people who know they're good enough, or who, "particularly the young," can afford to try and find out (2023).
- **You have no idea yet.** He wouldn't send you to Google to wait for one. He'd tell you not to hunt for ideas and to build side projects you want yourself, because that's where the good ideas come from.

**A different view within YC:** Dalton Caldwell and Michael Seibel (2026) say that if you can't find an ambitious idea, working at a company with high ambition can be better than spending years on a small startup. Their reason is to calibrate your ambition, not to learn how startups work. PG thinks ambition is mostly inborn, so he would point you back to doing it yourself.

Keep in mind that PG co-founded YC and has a stake in more people starting startups early. The vault's profile flags this bias.

**Verdict:** Paul Graham would most likely tell you to work on the hard, ambitious idea, but only if it's the one you're actually most interested in. He'd also tell you to start it small now rather than spend years earning money first. He would treat "an AI tool that makes money now" as a warning sign: picking work for the money is how you end up with plausible, mediocre ideas.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: high). He never compared these two options directly. But his rule about working on what interests you versus what pays appears in several sources, and his statements on money-hunting and ambition settle the question.

**How we get there**
1. He answers "follow your passion or work on what pays?" with a curve he calls a "midwit peak." If your main goal is moderate money, *"you can't usually afford to work on what interests you the most. People pay you for doing what they want, not what you want."* But *"if you want to become super rich, and you're young and good at technology, working on what you're most interested in becomes a good idea again."* And if you want to do great work, *"the complicated question … becomes simple. The answer is yes."* ([When To Do What You Love](https://paulgraham.com/when.html))
2. The rule behind this is in his thinking profile ([[thinking/pg]]): *"the best ideas tend to be such outliers that you'd overlook them if you were consciously looking for ways to make money."* ([same essay](https://paulgraham.com/when.html)) He says the same in his 2014 Stanford lecture: *"if you make a conscious effort to try and think of startup ideas, you will think of ideas that are not only bad, but bad and plausible sounding."* ([Before the Startup @ 24:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1474s))
3. "An AI tool that makes money now" is exactly that kind of consciously chosen, money-first idea. Which side of his curve you're on depends on your goal. If you're founding a startup, you're aiming at the high end of the curve, where interest wins.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Chasing money produces small gains.** *"Asking how the company could make more money is a good heuristic too, but it tends to yield incremental improvements."* He also sees a less ambitious idea as a symptom: *"the reason the idea is complicated is often fear. The company is unconsciously cowering by doing something less ambitious than they could."* ([Making Startups Powerful](https://paulgraham.com/powerful.html))
- **"Might take years" doesn't bother him.** He says founders don't run on dreams of wealth anyway: *"You put your head down and work on the model train set for 10 years."* ([PG on Startups, Ambition, and Great Founders @ 6:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=398s))
- **You don't need to fund the hard idea with an easy one first.** *"even a rocket startup you can start on not much money because what you do is you adjust for how much money you've got."* (@ [11:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=697s)) And: *"As long as you can get to some kind of milestone, then you can convince investors to give you more."* (@ [12:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=729s))
- **Take the risk early.** *"Take as much risk as you can afford; if you're not failing occasionally you're probably being too conservative,"* and *"take multiple shots. Which is another reason to start taking risks early."* ([Superlinear Returns](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html))
- **The ambitious idea still has to be something people want.** His fixed test is users and growth rate. Being hard is never a virtue by itself: *"you only prosper to the extend that you do"* ([Before the Startup @ 12:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=763s)).

Two other YC partners in the vault go further than PG on this. Caldwell and Seibel (August 2026) call low ambition "the secret killer of startups." Seibel's line is *"so hard to build a movement off of improving click-through rates by 1% by using AI."* ([Low Ambition is Killing Your Startup @ 10:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ozhRhElbVcI&t=656s))

**What would change his answer:**
- **You need the money or can't afford to fail.** He says high-variance paths are *"not for everyone. Most people will be better off as part of the pool"* ([Superlinear Returns](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html)). They suit people who are young or can afford to find out. If that isn't you, the money-now option is the sane choice on his own curve.
- **The ambitious idea appeals for prestige, not genuine interest.** He's against picking work for status as much as for pay.
- **The AI tool is what you're obsessed with and it's growing fast.** Then by his growth-rate test it *is* the startup. Many great ideas sound "lame" at first, and he'd tell you to ask what would make it more powerful.

The inference could break in one place: he never spoke about AI tools as a category. The answer applies his general rule about money-first ideas, not a statement about AI products.

**Verdict:** Focus on building. PG would say the product is how you impress people, and that writing is a tool for thinking. It isn't a growth channel or a way to look like a founder. Write when it helps you understand something. Don't post as a substitute for shipping.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). The vault has nothing from PG on whether founders should blog or post. The answer comes from his views on writing, on users vs. appearances, and on shipping speed.

**How we get there**
1. His closest statement is about words vs. prototypes: "The people you need to impress are users, not investors, and the way you impress them is with prototypes, not words." ([How Universities Should Prepare Founders](https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html), 2026)
2. The rule behind it, from his thinking page: make something people want. Tricks and appearances rank far below that. "There are tricks in the startups, as there are in any domain. But they are an order of magnitude less important than solving the real problem." ([Before the Startup](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=797s) @ 13:17)
3. Posting online to get attention or build a personal brand is one of those secondary things. So time spent on it while the product isn't shipping fast is time taken from the one thing that matters.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Shipping is still the bottleneck.** Even with AI tools: "there's still a lot of startups in this batch that are not shipping fast enough." ([PG on Startups, Ambition, and Great Founders](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=964s) @ 16:04, 2026)
- **Startups are a bad way to look good.** "If you want to seem cool, like starting a startup is just about the least efficient way to do it." (same talk @ 8:52) Posting to look like a successful founder has the same problem.
- **He's against selling brand in place of substance.** "it's probably a good idea not just to avoid buying brand, but to avoid selling it too." ([web-35ed22df6265], 2026)
- **But writing itself has real value, because writing is thinking.** "there's a kind of thinking that can only be done by writing." ([Writes and Write-Nots](https://paulgraham.com/writes.html), 2024) And: "trying to express what you understand is not just a way to prove that you understand it, but a way to understand it better." ([What to Do](https://paulgraham.com/do.html), 2025) So writing that sharpens your understanding of your users, market or product is worth doing, whether or not you publish it.
- **An audience does compound.** In 2023 he gave "growing an audience or brand" as an example of work that compounds ([Superlinear Returns](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html)). That is the strongest argument in the vault *for* posting. The vault's tensions page reads his 2023 and 2026 statements on brand as two different senses of the word. One is a reputation that grows because the work is good. The other is status sold in place of substance.

**What they've done:** Jessica Livingston says that when she met PG, he "he'd moved back to Cambridge after selling his startup via web to Yahoo and he was at the time writing essays" ([Livingston talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=375s) @ 6:15). So he wrote essays *after* his startup, not instead of building it. (Not in the vault: his 2005 essays and talks are widely credited with bringing in YC's first applicants. That was writing as an investor building a network, not as a founder looking for users.)

**A different YC view:** Caldwell and Seibel (2026) say press does "shockingly" little. They tell founders to post their own content directly, because it builds a channel to users and the same skills used in fundraising and recruiting ([yt-7TU636F_yVQ](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=1228s) @ 20:28). That's their view, not PG's. It also fits his rule: posting is fine when it reaches the people you're building for.

**What would change his answer:** If the writing *is* the go-to-market, he'd probably approve. That would be the case if your users read what you write (developer tools, technical products), or if writing helps you think through hard problems in your domain. The inference fails if the audience you build is made of your users and not of other founders and onlookers.

**Verdict:** Stay small. PG's position is that you should ideally be succeeding before you hire even two or three people, and that the seed money is for reaching the next milestone, not for building a team.

**Based on:** said it. His 2014 Stanford lecture covers early hiring directly. The seed-round angle follows from his 2026 remarks on making money last (confidence: high).

- **Hire late.** Asked about managing your first few people, he said: "ideally, you're successful before you even hire two or three people, right? Didn't you say, Sam, that Airbnb took five months to hire their first employee? So ideally, you don't have even two or three people for quite a while." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 34:44, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=2084s)
- **Management is a problem you earn, not one to set up early.** "management is a problem that you only have in a startup if you're sufficiently successful." What you need early on is "developing products." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 33:05)
- **Hire people you won't have to manage.** "the first hires in a startup are almost like founders. They should be motivated by the same things." "These have to be your peers, really. You shouldn't have to manage them much." Pick them "the way you would pick people if you were picking friends", people "you have known long enough to be sure." (@ 34:44, 35:18, 4:38) That kind of person is rare, so this rule slows hiring down on its own.
- **One exception.** He allows hiring a narrow specialist you have to support (his "boffin") if you really need what they know. (@ 35:52)
- **Use the money to reach a milestone.** In 2026 his advice is to "do what you can on the money you got. As long as you can get to some kind of milestone, then you can convince investors to give you more." ([[yt-5bxp78i96S8]] @ 12:09, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=729s) More people means more burn and less time to reach that milestone.

Startups still lose by not shipping fast enough, and he says the bottleneck is coming up with ideas, not the number of people producing things. ([[yt-5bxp78i96S8]] @ 16:04–16:38)

([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 25:10, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=1510s) That's her saying it, not PG.

He says it's a common way funded startups die, and that hiring before you have product-market fit usually means hoping people will fix a product that isn't working yet. Those essays aren't in the vault, so this is my paraphrase, not a quote.

For example, you can't keep up with demand, and a specific person you know well would fix that. Then you hire that person. That's hiring because you're succeeding, which is the order he recommends.

**Verdict:** Paul Graham would tell you to work on the idea you're passionate about, provided it's something real people want. He'd tell you to stop worrying about market size.

**Based on:** said it. He addressed both halves of the question separately. Putting them together is a small step, so confidence is high.

**Why he'd say it**

- **Interest matters most if you're aiming big.** In *When To Do What You Love* (2024, https://paulgraham.com/when.html) he describes a "midwit peak." If you only want a good income, you often can't afford to follow your interests. But "If you want to make a really huge amount of money — hundreds of millions or even billions of dollars — it turns out to be very useful to work on what interests you the most." He says the reason isn't motivation. It's that "the way to make a really large amount of money is to start a startup," and the biggest startups began as projects people did for fun.
- **Market size is the wrong thing to optimize early.** In *How to Earn a Billion Dollars* (2026, https://paulgraham.com/earn.html) he writes: "Don't worry about the second number, the market size. Since you predict future demand, the market will grow." He adds: "it's always possible to expand into adjacent markets. All you need is a beachhead in the territory of unsatisfied need that you can expand from." Seibel and Caldwell make the same point with Airbnb, Coinbase and Stripe, which all turned out far bigger than their founders expected.
- **Ideas picked because the market looks big are suspect.** "the best ideas tend to be such outliers that you'd overlook them if you were consciously looking for ways to make money" (when.html). Elsewhere he says that thinking up ideas on purpose produces ones that are "bad and plausible sounding."
- **Interest is required for exceptional work.** "to do something exceptionally well, you have to be interested in it. Mere diligence is not enough." (*Superlinear Returns*, 2023, https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html)
- **Pay attracts people who came for the pay.** "If you choose a kind of work mainly for how well it pays, you'll be surrounded by other people who chose it for the same reason" (when.html).

**Two checks he'd add**

1. **Make sure it's real interest.** His test: if this didn't pay, would you take a day job so you could keep doing it in your spare time? He warns that people often claim more interest than they have, because interest sounds better than wanting money.
2. **Passion doesn't replace users.** His core rule is still "make something people want." He thinks the passion idea is the better bet because you are your own first user. In his words, "usually young founders should make something that they themselves want." It still needs users who want it badly.

**If you're still torn:** he'd call that a sign you don't know enough yet: "When you can't decide which path to take, it's almost always due to ignorance." His fix is to build a rough version of the passion idea now, see whether anyone cares, and pick options that leave more options open, which he calls "staying upwind."

**What would change his answer:** He'd say the opposite if your goal is a solid income rather than a huge outcome. On that part of the curve, he says you usually can't afford to follow your interests. He'd also say the opposite if your "passion" is a topic you like that nobody has an unmet need for.

The vault has no tensions entry on this topic, so his 2024 and 2026 statements agree.

**Verdict:** Paul Graham would tell you to apply to YC. He'd also say that YC vs. angels matters much less than growth, because a startup that's growing fast can raise from anyone.

**Based on:** he said part of it directly and the rest follows from what he said (confidence: medium-high). He openly recommends doing YC. The vault doesn't have him comparing YC with an angel round head to head, so that part comes from applying his stated rules.

**How we get there**
1. **He recommends YC directly.** In a 2026 talk he says "Surely the optimal way to go to Silicon Valley for a bit and then come back is to do YC." He admits first: "I know it will sound like I'm talking my own book at this point" ([talk, May 2026 @ 17:16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1036s)).
2. **His main rule for fundraising** is that tricks matter far less than traction. "the best way to convince investors, is to start a startup that's actually doing well, meaning ... growing fast, and then simply tell investors so" ([2014 lecture @ 9:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=591s)). He also calls fundraising "merely a necessary evil. The people you need to impress are users, not investors" ([prepare.html](https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html)).
3. **Applying that rule:** a direct angel round means time spent fundraising instead of building. YC makes the fundraising faster and gives you peers and early customers. So for a founder who isn't already being chased by investors, he'd pick YC.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Investors take you more seriously.** "As soon as you tell them that you've been accepted by Y Combinator, often they're suddenly... they're tripping over themselves to try and invest in you" ([@ 6:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=399s)).
- **Investors decide faster.** "Even the speed at which investors have to decide is increased", and "you can do it all in like four to six months" ([@ 17:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1070s)).
- **The batch is worth more than the money.** "starting a startup is normally a very lonely business." When "you have some technical problem, probably somebody in the batch had that problem." And "you can sell it to the startups in your batch, no almost no matter what it is" ([Sept 2026 @ 17:11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=1031s)).
- **Don't bother learning how angel rounds work.** "Most of you don't know the mechanics of raising an Angel round... Mark Zuckerberg probably doesn't know the mechanics of raising an Angel round either" ([2014 @ 6:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=384s)).
- **Other YC partners agree.** Dalton Caldwell and Michael Seibel (Oct 2026) call months-long fundraises a waste. Caldwell: "it's way better to be like a very bad fundraiser ... with something that's working than someone that's a very good fundraiser with ... something that's not working at all" ([@ 5:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=335s)).

**What he's done:** He started YC as an angel firm. It was meant to fill the gap between VCs, who did giant late-stage rounds, and individual angels. The idea was to invest small amounts early, using standard paperwork.

**What would change his answer:** Fast growth. If you're already growing quickly and angels are chasing you, his own rule says the growth graph does the convincing and YC's fundraising help matters less. The batch and the peers would still count with him.

**Caveats:**
- He has an obvious stake in this answer: he co-founded YC, and he says so himself.
- The vault has nothing from him on what YC's deal costs you in equity compared with angel money. If that's what you're actually deciding, this answer doesn't cover it, and you should check YC's current terms.
- Applying to YC and talking to angels don't exclude each other. You can do both at once.

**Verdict:** Paul Graham would say you'd be better off with a co-founder, but you shouldn't stop and go looking for one first. Start building things now, with people you like and respect, and let the co-founder come out of that work. He thinks the best startups usually have more than one founder. He also thinks the only real test of a co-founder is working with them, so a planned search among strangers is the wrong way to find one.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). He said multiple founders tend to win and explained how co-founders find each other. He never answers "go solo or wait" in this vault.

**How we get there**
1. He thinks more than one founder is better. In his 2026 essay ([prepare.html](https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html)), the passage that gives the vault's quote ([[web-c75e015ff81a]]) also says: "The most successful startups tend to have multiple founders, and the only way to tell for sure if someone will be good to work with is to work with them. Apple and Microsoft were just the last of many projects their founders had worked on together." (That first sentence is from the raw essay; the wiki leaf leaves it out.)
2. In his view, co-founders come from projects, not from searching. His formula for getting startup ideas is "1, learn about things that matter. 2, work on problems that interest you. 3, with people you like and respect. That third part incidentally is how you get co-founders at the same time as the idea." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 25:41, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1541s))
3. He sets a high bar for who counts. "Work with people you genuinely like and respect ... and that you have known long enough to be sure. Because there's a lot of people who are really good at seeming likeable for a while." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 4:38, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=278s))
4. His habit is to learn by doing: "the best way to learn how to start a startup is to try and start it" ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 33:36, [[thinking/pg]]). So you'd start building now. If someone you've worked with well turns up along the way, you bring them in. You don't put the work on hold until a co-founder appears.

**Why he'd say it**
- He backs founders over ideas, especially "people who are good at building things and have a habit of doing it" ([[web-c75e015ff81a]]). Building with others is how you show that, and also how you find your co-founder.
- He'd also tell you to trust your instinct about people. If someone you've only just met doesn't feel right, don't partner with them: "one of the big mistakes that founders make is to not trust their intuitions about people enough." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 4:03)

**Outside the vault:** In his 2006 essay "18 Mistakes That Kill Startups," the first mistake he lists is having a single founder. He calls it a vote of no confidence (no friend would join you) and says it's too hard to carry alone. These essays haven't been ingested into the vault, so I'm paraphrasing rather than quoting.

**Where the rest of YC lands (for comparison)**

The solo founders who succeed build "co-founder-like" relationships to make up for it ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 2:11, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=131s)).

- Tan (2026) disagrees most: with AI agents, "before you have a co-founder or a logo or a deck, you can already be running an organization." ([[yt-eRrc1pUY5oU]] @ 21:20, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eRrc1pUY5oU&t=1280s)) PG's own view of AI is that it doesn't change the fundamentals: "so far almost everything is exactly the same" ([[yt-5bxp78i96S8]] @ 16:38).

**What would change his answer:** He'd back you going solo for now if your only options are people you haven't worked with or don't know well. By his rule, that's worse than starting alone.
